spec.title: Accepted requests per second (202/s) by sync mode
spec.description: The headline. Compare sync=on and sync=off in the 'over' phase (8000 req/s offered): I expect on to flatten near 4300 and off to reach a higher plateau. In the 'at' phase (4000 offered) both should sit at 4000. Surprising: off no higher than on (then the commit flush was not the limit). The counter k6_b6_resp_202_total is added by this experiment (k6 script); k6 series are not marked stale after a run, so the last value can linger for minutes.

spec.title: Latency p50 by sync mode
spec.description: Median latency of POST /v1/events seen by k6. Expect a drop in 'at' from about 5 ms (on) to about 2 ms (off). In 'over' runs p50 is dominated by queueing in front of the pool. Surprising: p50 not lower with off.

spec.title: Latency p99 by sync mode
spec.description: Tail latency. At 4000 req/s the 'on' mode is at about 93% utilisation of its capacity, so its p99 should be high (about 12-20 ms) while 'off' (about 70%) should be a few ms. Surprising: p99 of off higher than on.

spec.title: Not accepted (% of requests, 503 and other)
spec.description: Share of requests that did not get 202. Should be 0 in 'at' runs. In 'over' runs 503 (pool wait timeout) is expected for the excess. In the crash probes this jumps to 100% after the kill: that is expected. Uses k6_b6_resp_202_total, added by this experiment.

spec.title: Postgres up (pg_up)
spec.description: 1 = the postgres-exporter can reach Postgres. The dip to 0 is the docker kill of a crash probe, so this shows exactly when each probe killed the database and how long it took to answer again. Surprising: a dip in a measured run (then Postgres was restarted by something else).

spec.title: Requests answered 503 / other per second
spec.description: 503 is the pool timeout, 'other' (status 0) is connection refused or a client timeout. In crash probes 'other' should jump when the server is stopped after the kill. Added by this experiment (k6_b6_resp_503_total, k6_b6_resp_other_total).

spec.title: Query time (p50 / p99) seen by the server
spec.description: Time of one INSERT (including its COMMIT) as measured in Node. With on, almost all of it is the WAL flush (about 5 ms in B1). With off I expect it to fall to about 1-1.5 ms. This is the number that sets the pool bound 25 / hold time. Surprising: no change.

spec.title: Disk flush requests per second
spec.description: How often the host disk was asked to flush its write cache (node_disk_flush_requests_total, all devices). In B1 this was about 380/s with on. With off I expect under 50/s because only the WAL writer (every 200 ms) and checkpoints flush. Other processes on the host also flush, so a small floor is normal.

spec.title: Disk flushes per accepted request
spec.description: Flushes divided by 202/s. With on, several commits share one flush (group commit), so this is below 1. With off it should be close to 0. Meaningless between runs (division by about 0).

spec.title: Pool: in use, waiting
spec.description: Connections of the 25-connection pool that are busy, and requests waiting for one. With on at the knee the pool is full and the wait grows. With off the pool should be far from full at the same rate because every connection is released sooner. Surprising: pool full with off.

spec.title: Commits per second (Postgres)
spec.description: pg_stat_database_xact_commit rate. Should equal the accepted rate (one INSERT, one commit). A gap with 202/s would mean extra transactions. The postgres-exporter scrapes every few seconds, so short runs look coarse.

spec.title: WAL written per second
spec.description: ep_pg_wal_bytes_total rate (from pg-wal-exporter.sh, which stops working after the first crash probe, so only measured runs show here). The WAL volume per row should be the same for on and off: off changes WHEN WAL is flushed, not how much is written.

spec.title: Postgres container CPU (cores)
spec.description: From pg-container-exporter.sh (stops after the first kill). The container has 2 cores. With off the INSERT work goes up (more rows/s) but waiting is gone. Surprising: near 2 cores (then Postgres CPU would be the limit, not Node).

spec.title: Node CPU (cores, ingest-api)
spec.description: process_cpu_seconds_total of the server. Node runs JS on one thread, so about 1.0 = saturated. My prediction is that off is limited by this at about 5500 req/s. Surprising: far below 1 core while rps is flat (then something else limits).

spec.title: Disk busy (%util)
spec.description: node_disk_io_time_seconds_total rate x 100 for the busiest device. B1 saw about 97% with on. With off it should drop a lot. Several devices on the host: the busiest one is shown.

spec.title: In-flight requests (server)
spec.description: http_requests_in_flight. By Little's Law this is rate x latency. Grows when requests queue in front of the pool.

spec.title: Host CPU by pinned group (%)
spec.description: Busy CPU of each pinned group (server, postgres, k6, monitoring) from node_exporter. Follows the cpu_* variables. Keep the k6 group under about 70% so the generator is not the limit.

spec.title: Postgres connections by state
spec.description: pg_stat_activity_count by state. Expect up to 25 'active'/'idle in transaction' from the pool plus the exporter's 1.

spec.title: k6 dropped iterations per second
spec.description: Must be 0 in 'at' runs. In 'over' runs drops are expected (that is how saturation looks). Surprising: drops in an 'at' run (then the generator or the server could not keep 4000 req/s).

spec.title: k6 VUs in use
spec.description: Virtual users. If it reaches the max (3000) in an 'at' run the generator ran out of users. 'over' runs may use many.

spec.title: k6 CPU group (%)
spec.description: The CPUs k6 is pinned to. Keep under about 70%: above that the generator may be the limit, and a capacity number is not valid.

spec.title: Server CPU group (%)
spec.description: The CPUs Node is pinned to (0,6). Node uses one thread, so about 50% of this two-CPU group means one thread fully busy. Compare with the Node cores panel.

spec.title: 1. The verdict: did synchronous_commit change throughput and latency?
2. The mechanism: where did the commit wait go?
3. Resource view: where does the cost land?
4. Validity: can I trust this run?
